title: Evaluate
summary: Pick the question whose answer would decide whether the argument holds. Test each choice with two answers: one should help, the other should hurt.

slides.title: The question that settles it
body: Evaluate answers are questions or pieces of information to look up. The right one targets the gap: depending on how it is answered, the argument gets stronger or weaker.
A choice whose answer wouldn’t matter either way is wrong, however interesting it sounds.
slides.callout: Answer the question both ways. If one answer helps and the other hurts, you’ve found it.

slides.title: How you’ll see it
stems: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the argument?
Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
In order to evaluate the argument, it would be most helpful to determine which one of the following?

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.do: Same as weaken and strengthen: what does the argument take for granted?

steps.label: Predict
steps.do: Phrase a question about that assumption: did anything else change? Is the sample typical?

steps.label: Answer it both ways
steps.do: For each choice, imagine a yes and a no. Does one help the argument and the other hurt it?

steps.label: Drop the neutral ones
steps.do: If neither answer changes how strong the argument is, the choice is out.

slides.title: Level 1: the method, step by step
slides.stimulus: Since the town of Ferris lowered the speed limit on Route 9 from 55 to 45 miles per hour, the number of accidents on Route 9 has dropped by a third. The town council concludes that the lower speed limit made Route 9 safer.
slides.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the council's conclusion?

choices.A: Do most drivers in Ferris approve of the lower speed limit?
choices.B: How many miles long is Route 9?
choices.C: Did the amount of traffic on Route 9 fall during the same period?
choices.D: Are speed limits on other roads in Ferris also 45 miles per hour?
choices.E: Has the town council lowered speed limits on other roads in the past?

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.note: The lower limit made the road safer: a causal claim.
steps.highlight: the lower speed limit made Route 9 safer

steps.label: Gap
steps.note: Fewer accidents could have another cause, like less traffic.

steps.label: Answer C both ways
steps.note: Yes, traffic fell: the drop may be due to fewer cars, so the argument weakens. No: the drop is more likely due to the limit, so it strengthens.

steps.label: Check the rest
steps.note: Approval, road length, other roads and past decisions don’t change the strength of the argument however they are answered.

why.A: Approval doesn't bear on whether the road became safer.
why.B: Length is the same before and after, so it doesn't explain the change.
why.C: Correct. A yes weakens the causal conclusion; a no supports it.
why.D: Other roads' limits don't explain what happened on Route 9.
why.E: The council's history doesn't affect whether this change worked.

slides.title: Level 2: a before-and-after claim with no comparison group
slides.stimulus: Dr. Okafor: Of the patients at the Larkspur clinic who completed a six-week mindfulness course, nearly all rated their stress as much lower at the end of the course than at the start. Patients rated their stress on a standard ten-point scale at the first and last sessions. Many of them also said they felt more in control of their daily lives. I conclude that taking the course lowers a patient's stress.
slides.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating Dr. Okafor's conclusion?

choices.A: Were the course sessions held in the morning rather than in the evening, and at the same hour each week?
choices.B: Was the fee for the course higher than the fees other clinics charge for similar courses?
choices.C: Has the Larkspur clinic offered a course like this one in earlier years?
choices.D: Is the method taught in the course also taught in clinics in other countries?
choices.E: Did the stress ratings of patients who did not take the course also fall over the same six weeks?

steps.label: Find the conclusion
steps.note: The course lowers stress.
steps.highlight: taking the course lowers a patient's stress

steps.label: Find the evidence
steps.note: Stress ratings were lower at the end than at the start.
steps.highlight: rated their stress as much lower at the end of the course than at the start

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.note: The claim is before and after, with no comparison group. Stress may fall over six weeks even without the course.

steps.label: Answer E both ways
steps.note: Yes, ratings fell for people who did not take it: the drop is not due to the course, so the argument weakens. No: the course looks like the cause, so it strengthens.

steps.label: Drop the neutral ones
steps.note: Session time, fee, past courses and use abroad do not change how strong the argument is, however they are answered.

why.A: Neither answer changes whether the course lowered stress.
why.B: Fees at other clinics do not bear on the effect of this course.
why.C: Whether earlier courses existed is neutral either way.
why.D: Use in other countries does not show what happened to these patients.
why.E: Correct. A yes weakens the causal claim and a no supports it.

slides.title: Level 3: allows is not the same as will serve
slides.stimulus: Consultant: The Bellmont County library system should replace its printed periodical subscriptions with digital ones. Each printed copy is read by an average of about three patrons before it is discarded. A digital license, by contrast, allows any number of patrons to read the periodical at the same time, and it costs only 20 percent more than a printed subscription. The system's board has asked for a recommendation based on cost per patron served. Clearly, then, each dollar spent on a digital subscription will serve more patrons than each dollar spent on a printed one.
slides.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the consultant's argument?

choices.A: Do other library systems of similar size spend more per patron on periodicals than the Bellmont County system does at present?
choices.B: Would most of the patrons who now read the printed copies be willing to read the same periodicals on a screen?
choices.C: Is the price of a digital license lower than the price that other library systems pay for the same periodicals?
choices.D: Do the periodicals that the system subscribes to include more weekly titles than monthly titles?
choices.E: Does the board plan to review its periodical subscriptions again within the next five years?

steps.label: Find the conclusion
steps.note: Digital serves more patrons per dollar.
steps.highlight: each dollar spent on a digital subscription will serve more patrons than each dollar spent on a printed one

steps.label: Find the evidence
steps.note: Digital allows unlimited readers at a small price premium.
steps.highlight: allows any number of patrons to read the periodical at the same time

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.note: Allows is not will serve. The argument counts everyone who could read a digital copy as a patron served. It assumes the current readers will actually use a screen.

steps.label: Answer B both ways
steps.note: Yes, most would: digital reaches many patrons and the claim holds. No, few would: digital serves fewer patrons per dollar and the claim fails.

steps.label: Name the traps
steps.note: A and C are about money and other systems. The prices are already given, so either answer leaves the comparison as it was. D and E are neutral too.

why.A: Other systems' spending does not change the cost per patron served here.
why.B: Correct. A yes supports the claim and a no undermines it, because the count of patrons served depends on this.
why.C: The prices are already given in the argument, so what other systems pay changes nothing.
why.D: The mix of weekly and monthly titles does not alter the comparison either way.
why.E: The board's review schedule does not affect cost per patron served.

slides.title: Level 4: before or after? One word decides
slides.stimulus: Auditor's report: Last year the city audited twenty-four of its departments. Each of the nine audited departments that had adopted the new purchasing software in the preceding two years had a lower rate of billing errors than the average for all twenty-four audited departments. The software was available to every department, and each department's head chose whether to adopt it. The software vendor offered the same terms to every department. The auditors counted every billing error found in each department's records for the year. We can conclude that adopting the software reduces a department's rate of billing errors.
slides.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the auditor's conclusion?

choices.A: After adopting the software, did the nine adopting departments have lower billing-error rates than the audited average?
choices.B: Did the software cost the city more to buy and to install than the purchasing system it replaced?
choices.C: Did the heads of the nine departments that adopted the software say, when asked, that they were satisfied with it?
choices.D: Before adopting the software, did the nine adopting departments already have lower billing-error rates than the audited average?
choices.E: Were all twenty-four of the audited departments audited during the same month of last year?

steps.label: Find the conclusion
steps.note: Adopting the software cuts billing errors.
steps.highlight: adopting the software reduces a department's rate of billing errors

steps.label: Find the evidence
steps.note: The adopters had lower error rates than the audited average.
steps.highlight: had a lower rate of billing errors than the average for all twenty-four audited departments

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.note: Each head chose whether to adopt. Departments with few errors may have been the ones to adopt, so the low rates may predate the software.
steps.highlight: each department's head chose whether to adopt it

steps.label: Answer D both ways
steps.note: Yes, they were already lower: the software may have done nothing, so the argument weakens. No: the low rates came after adoption, so it strengthens.

steps.label: Name the one-word trap
steps.note: A swaps Before for After. The stimulus already says the adopters were lower at the audit, so no answer to A can change anything.

steps.label: Drop the neutral ones
steps.note: Cost, satisfaction and audit timing do not bear on whether the software caused the low rates.

why.A: Answered already in the stimulus. The word After makes it useless, since the adopters' lower rates at the audit are given.
why.B: Cost does not bear on whether the software reduced errors.
why.C: Opinions of the heads do not show what caused the error rates, whichever way they are answered.
why.D: Correct. A yes shows self-selection and weakens the argument. A no supports it.
why.E: The timing of audits is neutral for the claim about the software.

slides.title: Cheat card
lines: Find the gap first, as for weaken and strengthen.
Answer each choice yes and no.
One answer helps, the other hurts: that’s the one.
